## From: Hallam-Baker, Phillip  Time: 14:00  Subject: RE: Ah, I see the cause of the situation now... (tls-authz situation)

I think Melinda makes a good point here.

The fundamental problem with these RMS-grams is that RMS has a longstanding habit of working in write only mode. He makes little or often no effort to determine what the situation is. I have in the past found him entirely interested in responding to enquires as to the purpose of his campaigns.

RMS has a certain number of supporters who are willing to write letters. That does not mean that RMS's opinion should hold greater weight than that of other people.

As I have argued in the past, the IETF should have an IPR policy precisely because of this type of situation. I do not see why there should be a need to reopen this debate every single time RMS wants to reopen it.

I suggest that we first eliminate from consideration all the submissions which make no reference to the specific TLS-Authz document in question. In other words, the one liners of the form 'standards should not have patents' without making any reference to this specific document all go in the bit bucket. If on the other hand it is of the form 'we at the FSF have an implementation that a lot of people use...' then that is different

________________________________

From: [email] on behalf of Melinda Shore Sent: Tue 2/10/2009 4:29 PM To: Alex Loret de Mola; Ole Jacobsen Cc: [email] Subject: Re: Ah, I see the cause of the situation now... (tls-authz situation)

*I* feel that the individuals posting here were largely clueless.  What, the "Reject TLS!" post didn't raise your eyebrows?

I think the problem here is that the FSF issued an action alert that contained an awful lot of misinformation, and its minions did what they were asked - they posted an "opinion" of a document they clearly hadn't read.

This was an effort by another organization to get a large number of IETF nonparticipants to send email to the IETF.  I understand that we want to encourage people to be interested in our documents and let us know what they think but for heaven's sake they deserve to be dismissed out-of-hand if they haven't even bothered to read the thing for which they're trying to block publication.

Melinda

## From: Steven M. Bellovin  Time: 14:19  Subject: Re: why to contact the IETF

On Tue, 10 Feb 2009 10:59:52 -0800 "Lawrence Rosen" <[email]> wrote:

No, they didn't raise the concern.  The concern had been raised previously by people who are obviously IETF participants, including Simon Josefsson.  (I don't recall if you've posted on this particular I-D, but I obviously put you in the category of IETF participant, too.)

As you well know, the IETF per se doesn't care about the answer to that question.  Individual participants may care, of course, and can and should use that information when making their own judgments.

More precisely -- the statement "the IETF should not standardize draft-chthulhu-shogoth-666.txt because the technology is patented" is a NOP according to IETF policies on patented works.  The proper formulation is "I feel that standardizing draft-chthulhu-shogoth-666.txt is a bad idea because in this particular case, the licensing terms are too onerous for the benefit gained", perhaps with a suggestion that some other technology be adopted instead.

Absolutely -- that's everyone's right, privilege, and (arguably) duty. I haven't looked at it myself because I have no particular interest in it at the moment, but this is definitely the proper course.  It's also perfectly proper to post analyses to influence others -- that was done years ago in IPsec to reassure people that a particular patent was unlikely to be enforceable.

--Steve Bellovin, http://www.cs.columbia.edu/~smb

## From: Ofer Inbar  Time: 14:23  Subject: Re: ideological opposition to patents

Powers Chuck-RXCP20 <[email]> wrote:

I think software patents are a bad idea, and would prefer that there be none of them.  I think software is like music, and patenting software is like patenting chords or melodies.  Patents are the wrong legal tool for software, and they undermine the purpose of IPR (which is to promote "progress" of the "useful arts").

Nevertheless, I see no reason to oppose standardizing a protocol that is unencumbered by patents, simply because some uses of that protocol (even if they may be common) are encumbered.

I think such opposition requires more than mere opposition to software patents, or to patents in general.  At the very least, it also requires that one not think through the logical consequences of one's strategy.

In practice, however, I believe most of the people who sent us drive-by mailings were simply misinformed or mistaken about the facts. -- Cos

## From: Noel Chiappa  Time: 14:24  Subject: RE: why to contact the IETF

That point could have been raised _much_ more efficiently with a single email message from someone such as yourself.

I'm not sure I'd really believe any determination short of a court's anyway - attorneys can advise, but until the proverbial butcher-baker-candlestickmaker get their say after a trial, it's got an element of coin-toss to it, no?

Taking no strong position on this particular specification (which is not in my area of interest), but, as a general observation, nothing says anyone has to use any particular IETF specification. If you don't want to mess with a potential patent hassle, just don't use it.

The IETF is just a place to create standards in an open way, and it seems there is some open community of experts interested in this area who seem to have determined that the advantages of using an encumbered solution here outweigh the disadvantages.

An effective critique of that judgement _does not_ mean just saying 'encumbered technology is bad', because most of us already agree with that general statement. One would have to understand the details of why they felt that that the advantages of using this particular encumbered solution outweighed the obvious disadvantages, and show where the problem with that reasoning was.

Alternatively, if there are a community of people who see a need, and don't like using a patent-encumbered solution, they can create an alternative not so hampered - and the IETF would, I would expect, be happy to afford them an open forum to do so.

Noel

## From: Marshall Eubanks  Time: 14:33  Subject: Re: why to contact the IETF

In my experience, attorneys will almost never give hard answers to questions like this. And it typically takes a few million dollars in coins to make a toss.

Regards Marshall

<speaking as an individual, not wearing any hats>

What does it mean for the IETF to be an open forum for developing standards, even when patent concerns exist?

chosen.content: It means the IETF provides an open process where anyone in the community can discuss, critique, and help develop standards, even if some technologies involved may be patented. In that process, participants can raise patent concerns, evaluate whether the benefits outweigh the drawbacks, and even propose alternative unencumbered solutions. However, the IETF itself does not reject a standard simply because it uses patented technology; the decision is based on the community’s judgment of the tradeoffs.

**Relevance**: **High** – Reveals the strategic reasoning behind the technical solution: RFC 9685 has active use cases (Wi-SUN) while RFC 8928 appears unused, making it the logical candidate for updating.

---

**Context Marker**: Concluding procedural decision that summarizes the scheduling approach for this Internet-Draft.

**Relevance**: **Medium** – Captures the final administrative action being taken, though less critical to understanding the technical substance.

**Relationship**: Represents the logical conclusion of the reasoning in Extract 3; implements the efficiency strategy motivated by the document's simplicity (Extract 1) and clear resolution path (Extract 2).

What role did the Wi-SUN use case play in the decision-making process for resolving the IANA registration overlap?

chosen.content:
The Wi-SUN use case played a **decisive role** in determining which RFC would be updated to resolve the IANA registration overlap.

## Key Decision Factor

The document explicitly states that **RFC 9685 is intended to be used by Wi-SUN**, while **nobody in the 6LO WG knows about any use of RFC 8928**. This contrast in deployment status became the primary justification for the resolution approach.

## Impact on the Decision

The Wi-SUN use case influenced the decision in the following way:

1. **Protected the active implementation**: Since RFC 9685 had an identified, active use case (Wi-SUN), modifying it would potentially disrupt real-world deployments

2. **Identified the path of least resistance**: With RFC 8928 having no known implementations, it became the logical candidate for updating without causing operational impact

3. **Informed stakeholder consensus**: The decision was made collectively by the 6LO WG, Area Director (AD), and IANA, with the Wi-SUN use case serving as a concrete reason to preserve RFC 9685 as-is

## Conclusion

The Wi-SUN use case essentially acted as a **tiebreaker** in the decision-making process. When faced with two RFCs in conflict, the presence of an active, identified deployment for RFC 9685 made updating RFC 8928 the clear and practical choice to resolve the IANA registration overlap.

### Abstract Conceptual Layer Summary

**Overarching Themes:**
1. **Federated Sign-On Protocol**: Focus on secure identity token issuance and usage between Identity Providers, clients, and Relying Parties.
2. **Token Binding for Security**: Enhancing security by binding identity tokens to TLS connections, ensuring tokens are used only by the intended client.
3. **Federation Scenarios**: Generalized process of token issuance and consumption, emphasizing security through token binding.

**Main Arguments:**
1. **Identity Token Security**: Using TLS binding of identity tokens to restrict their use to the issuing client, as seen in protocols like OpenID Connect and SAML.
2. **Token Binding Protocol**: Utilizing the Token Binding protocol to associate tokens with a client's specific TLS connection, preventing misuse by unauthorized parties.
3. **Token Consumer and Provider Interaction**: Token Consumers request token binding to ensure tokens are tied to the legitimate client, with Token Providers embedding the Token Binding ID in the token.

**Core Principles:**
1. **Authentication and Authorization**: Identity tokens authenticate clients to Relying Parties, with token binding providing an additional security layer.
2. **Token Binding Mechanism**: The Token Binding ID, derived from a client's key pair, is used to verify the legitimacy of token usage by comparing it with the TLS connection's Token Binding ID.
3. **Communication of Token Binding ID**: Token Binding IDs are communicated from the client to the Token Provider during token requests, ensuring the token is bound to the client's identity.

**Details:**
- **Identity Token Binding**: The Identity Provider binds identity tokens to the client's TLS connection to ensure secure authentication with the Relying Party.
- **Token Consumer's Role**: Token Consumers request token binding to ensure tokens are used only by the intended client, leveraging the Token Binding protocol.
- **Token Provider's Responsibility**: Token Providers issue tokens with embedded Token Binding IDs, linking them to the client's key pair for secure usage verification.
- **Redirect-Based Federation Protocols**: Mechanisms for Token Consumers to signal token binding requests are specified for protocols involving redirects from Token Consumers to Token Providers.

How do Redirect-Based Federation Protocols facilitate token binding requests?

chosen.content:
In the provided document, Redirect-Based Federation Protocols facilitate token binding requests through specific mechanisms that enable Token Consumers to signal their desire for token binding to the Token Providers. This is typically done in scenarios where the Token Consumer (such as a client application) initiates a redirect to the Token Provider (such as an Identity Provider) to request an identity token. 

Here’s how the process works:

1. **Initiation of Redirect**: The Token Consumer initiates a redirect to the Token Provider. This redirect includes specific parameters or headers that indicate the request for token binding.

2. **Token Binding Request**: During this redirect, the Token Consumer communicates its intention to have the identity tokens bound to its specific TLS connection. This request effectively asks the Token Provider to include a Token Binding ID in the identity token.

3. **Token Binding ID Communication**: The Token Binding ID, which is derived from the client's key pair, is communicated from the Token Consumer to the Token Provider. This ID ensures that the token is securely bound to the client's identity and the specific TLS connection being used.

4. **Token Issuance with Binding**: The Token Provider, upon receiving the token binding request, issues the identity token with the embedded Token Binding ID. This binding ensures that the token can only be used by the client that initiated the request and is protected against misuse by unauthorized parties.

5. **Verification and Usage**: When the client uses the token to authenticate with a Relying Party, the Token Binding ID in the token is compared with the Token Binding ID of the current TLS connection. This verification step ensures that the token is being used in the context of the original, legitimate client's connection.

By following these steps, Redirect-Based Federation Protocols ensure that identity tokens are securely bound to the intended client, enhancing the overall security of federated authentication processes.

What role does a reference to the Multicast Source Discovery Protocol (MSDP) play in a MIB specification for multicast source discovery?

chosen.content:
In this MIB specification, the reference to the **Multicast Source Discovery Protocol (MSDP)** serves as a **normative reference** that defines the actual protocol the MIB is managing.

Put simply:

- The **MIB** describes how to **monitor and manage** multicast source discovery via SNMP.
- The **MSDP specification** (RFC 3618) provides the **protocol behavior, terminology, and semantics** that the MIB objects relate to.
- Therefore, the MSDP reference is essential because it tells implementers **what protocol the MIB is modeling and instrumenting**.

So, the MSDP reference plays the role of the **authoritative protocol definition underlying the MIB for multicast source discovery**.

1. **An interconnection node's forwarding actions are modeled as a concatenation of an egress node functional model and an ingress node functional model.**
  → This explains the theoretical framework used to describe how traffic moves through a node that connects two different rings.

2. **The egress model handles traffic exiting a ring, while the ingress model handles traffic entering a ring.**
  → This clarifies the specific roles of the two functional models mentioned in the concatenation process.

3. **Interconnection nodes F and A both belong to Ring 1 and Ring 2.**
  → This establishes the topology of the network, identifying F and A as the shared points between the two ring structures.

4. **Node A is an adjacent node to node F in both rings.**
  → Because both nodes are members of both rings, they maintain a neighbor relationship across both network segments.

5. **The process for packets entering node F from Ring 1 involves a label pop, a label swap, and a label push.**
  → This summarizes the three-step label manipulation sequence required to transition traffic from one ring's tunnel to another.

6. **The ring tunnel label [R1cW\_F&A(F)] is popped when packets are received from the West ring port of Ring 1.**
  → This is the first step of the forwarding process, removing the outer ring tunnel identifier upon arrival at the interconnection node.

7. **The MPLS packet label [LSP1(F&A)] is swapped to [LSP1(I)] via the MT LSP sub-layer.**
  → This is the second step, where the internal LSP label is updated to reflect the next hop (Node I) from the perspective of the MT layer.

8. **The ring tunnel label [R2cW\_I(G)] is pushed before the traffic enters Ring 2.**
  → This is the final step, adding the necessary ring tunnel label for the destination ring to ensure proper routing.

9. **MPLS-TP section layer OAM monitors connectivity between adjacent ring nodes.**
  → This identifies the specific tool (Operations, Administration, and Maintenance) used to ensure the physical/logical links are active.

10. **Connectivity monitoring follows mechanisms defined in [IETF RFC 6371].**
  → This provides the industry standard reference for how the OAM monitoring is implemented.

11. **Defect conditions on MPLS-TP sections are detected according to [ITU-T G.8121].**
  → This specifies the standard used to determine if a section of the network is malfunctioning.

12. **For MSRP switching, a ring span is classified as either "OK" or "failed (SF)".**
  → This simplifies the complex state of a link into a binary condition to trigger protection switching.

13. **SF is declared when the MT\_TT\_Sk function of an MPLS-TP section MEP detects a trail signal fail.**
  → This describes the technical trigger (a signal failure at the trail termination sink) that leads to a "failed" status.

14. **A node failure is defined as the failure of the two links attached to that node.**
  → This clarifies that a node is considered "down" when both its ingress and egress links are detected as failed by adjacent nodes.

15. **Provisionable hold-off timers coordinate protection switching for nested protection.**
  → These timers prevent premature switching in complex environments where multiple layers of protection might overlap.

16. **The suggested range for hold-off timers is 0 to 10 seconds in 100 ms steps.**
  → This provides the specific configuration parameters available to network administrators for tuning the timers.

17. **The RPS protocol controls MSRP protection operations.**
  → This identifies the Ring Protection Switch (RPS) protocol as the control mechanism for the MSRP process.

18. **RPS requests, PDU formats, and ring node states are specified in [IETF RFC 8227].**
  → This directs the reader to the external standard that defines the actual messaging and state machine of the RPS protocol.

In the concatenation process, which functional model is tasked with managing traffic entering a ring?

chosen.content: The ingress model handles traffic entering a ring.

**Relationship**: Sets up the contrast/transition from MPLS to IPv6; directly supports the focus on “SR over an IPv6 data plane” stated in Extract 3.

**Relevance**: **Very High** — Explicitly identifies the deliverable and the exact problem the draft addresses.  
**Relationship**: Builds on Extracts 1 and 2: SR’s definition (Extract 1) and its IPv6 instantiation (Extract 2) culminate in the need for OSPFv3 extensions (this extract).

Segment Routing (SR) defines an end-to-end path as what kind of sequence, and what are the elements of that sequence called?

chosen.content: Segment Routing (SR) defines an end-to-end path as a **sequence of topological sub-paths**, and the elements of that sequence are called **“segments.”**

How does the call sign of a radio station help in its identification?

chosen.content:
The call sign of a radio station serves as a unique identifier that helps in its recognition and identification, akin to a name. Here's how it aids in the identification process:

1. **Uniqueness**: Each radio station has a distinct call sign that distinguishes it from other stations. This uniqueness ensures that there is no confusion between different broadcasts across various regions or frequencies.

2. **Regulation and Licensing**: The call sign is assigned and regulated by national authorities (such as the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) in the United States). It is part of the licensing process that confirms the station's legal operation.

3. **Inter-state and International Navigation**: Call signs can provide information about where a station is located or where it originates. For example, certain call sign prefixes are allocated by country, which can help identify the station's country of origin.

4. **Listener Recognition**: Regular listeners often recognize stations by their call sign, which can become a part of the station's brand and identity. It is used in advertising and promotional material.

5. **Emergency Broadcast Identification**: In times of emergency, call signs play a critical role in broadcasting local alerts and information.

Overall, the call sign acts as a crucial tool for identifying, regulating, and branding a radio station.

messages.content:
# R3-070965

- **Agenda Item:** 13.2.2.3

- **Source:** Motorola

- **Title:** Paging load reduction in synchronized cells

- **Document for:** Discussion and Approval

## # 1. Introduction

In this contribution, we introduce a paging scheme for UEs that is applicable in cells that are time-synchronized. The proposed scheme offers significant reduction in paging load without impacting the battery life of the UE or the paging delay. Note that mixed cells in LTE offering both MBMS and unicast services in SFN mode are expected to be time-synchronized. Therefore, the scheme discussed in this paper can be utilized in all those cells.

## # 2. Cascaded paging

In idle mode, a paging channel (PCH) is assigned to the UE and the UE wakes up to check for any page message in that resource. In case there are multiple PCHs in a cell, the UE shall be assigned to one of them. The paging scheme proposed here is mainly motivated by the fact that UEs are typically found with a high probability at the last known cell, where it performed a tracking area update (TAU) or ended its last call. From field statistics, a mobile can be found in the same cell as was last observed in, approximately 50% to 90% of the time.

Based on this, it is proposed to page the UE in a sequential fashion. However, normal sequential paging may result in a longer paging delay when the UE is not present in the area in which it is paged first. As a result, it is important to design a paging scheme that provides the benefits of reduced paging load offered by sequential paging without introducing considerable delay. In our proposal, when a call arrives for the UE, the UE is initially paged only in its last known cell as shown in Figure 1. In case there is no response, the UE is paged in the remaining cells of the tracking area after a finite time duration *T* (e.g., 100 ms). The value of *T* includes the timeout required at the last known eNB to figure out that the UE has not responded.

In current systems, the PCH assigned to a UE is statically determined as a function of its IMSI. To perform fast re-paging, the PCH allocation must be more dynamic. In the scheme proposed in this paper, the PCH assigned to the UE in the remaining cells of the tracking area depends on the PCH allocated to the UE in its last known cell. For example, as illustrated in Figure 2, if the UE is assigned PCH1 in its last known cell and if PCH1 occurs at times t, t+5, t+10, etc., then the PCH implicitly assigned to the UE in the new cell is the one that occurs immediately after t+T, t+5+T, t+10+T (e.g., PCH2 in the new cell).

When the UE is in its last known cell, it wakes up to listen to PCH1 and when it moves out to a new cell, the UE automatically wakes up to listen to a different PCH based on its knowledge of the timing of PCH1 in the last known cell. This implicit determination of the PCH slot requires that the eNBs are time-synchronized. Because the value of *T* is expected to be small, the paging delay introduced due to this sequential paging is not significant. After paging the UE in the first cell, the source eNB informs the UE of the result of the paging. In case of failure, the MME informs the remaining cells to page for the UE.

From field statistics, at the time of a page to the mobile, the UE can be found in the same cell where the UE was last observed, between ~50% to 90% of the time. This yields that the paging load is reduced by ~2x to 10x; or $S/(P*1+(1-P)*S) \approx 1/(1-P)$ where:

- * P = probability mobile is still in the same cell was last observed in

- * S = number of cells in paging area

## ## 3. Conclusions

We request that RAN3 discuss the above scheme and agree with the proposed fast cascaded paging as it provides a significant reduction in paging load. We also propose to include a statement in TS 36.300 as shown in the text proposal below:

## ***************************START OF CHANGES***************************

## ### 19.2.2.1 Paging procedure

The MME initiates the paging procedure by sending the PAGING message to each eNB belonging to the tracking area(s) in which the UE is registered. Sequential paging techniques that do not introduce significant paging delays will be considered.

The paging response back to the MME is initiated on NAS layer and is sent by the eNodeB based on NAS-level routing information.

## ***************************END OF CHANGES***************************

How does the paging load reduction scheme ensure that the paging delay remains negligible?

chosen.content:
The paging load reduction scheme described in the document ensures that the paging delay remains negligible through its strategic approach to sequentially paging the User Equipment (UE) primarily based on its last known location, with additional mechanisms in place for quick transition to the remaining cells if necessary. Here's a breakdown of how the scheme achieves this:

1. **Initial Paging in Last Known Cell**: The proposed scheme begins by pinging the UE exclusively in its last known cell, where it is statistically most likely to be found (50% to 90% probability). By exploiting this high probability, the scheme minimizes the delay by avoiding the need to page in all cells immediately.

2. **Sequential Paging with Timeout**: If the UE does not respond in its last known cell within a specified short duration (*T*, e.g., 100 ms), the paging is extended to other cells in the tracking area. The short duration of *T* is critical as it prevents excessive delay, allowing almost immediate paging in other cells if the UE is not in the last known one.

3. **Dynamic PCH Allocation**: To efficiently page UEs in new cells, the scheme uses an implicit, dynamic allocation of Paging Channel (PCH) timing based on the last known cell's PCH timing. This mechanism ensures that a UE immediately begins listening on the correct slot once moved to a new cell, leveraging time-synchronized eNodeBs without introducing a significant time lags.

4. **Minimal Delay in Paging**: The scheme intentionally keeps the value of *T* small, minimizing the delay caused by the sequential paging approach. This strategic timeout balances the trade-off between reducing paging load and maintaining low paging delay.

5. **Feedback Mechanism**: After an initial failed paging in the first cell, the Mobile Management Entity (MME) quickly informs the remaining cells, allowing for rapid further paging attempts across the tracking area without significant additions to the delay.

By combining the high likelihood of finding the UE in its last known location with this methodical and dynamically timed approach to paging in the rest of the region, the scheme efficiently reduces paging loads by factors of up to 10x while keeping the associated paging delays minimal and manageable.
